newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian targeted in probe of Paris train bombing.
newsitem.headline: Algerian targeted in probe of Paris train bombing.

text.p: An Algerian man has been formally placed under investigation on suspicion of helping to organise a 1995 bomb attack on a Paris subway train in which eight people died, French judges told victims' relatives on Friday.

They said Boualem Bensaid, the first suspect to be officially targeted in the two-year-old probe, was believed to have been the ringleader of the group which bombed the RER underground train at Saint Michel station in central Paris on July 25, 1999.

Nearly 100 people were injured in the attack, the first of a series in 1995 and 1996 blamed by investigators on Algerian fundamentalist rebels angry at France's backing for the government of its former colony.

Being placed under investigation in France is a preliminary step to a trial but does not imply guilt and does not necessarily lead to a trial. Individuals are not formally charged in France before being brought to trial.

The step was disclosed to victims' relatives at the law courts building in central Paris by judges leading the investigation of the bombing, said Francoise Rudetzki, president of the victims rights group SOS-Attentats.
Anti-terrorism judges Jean-Francois Ricard and Jean-Louis Bruguiere had briefed a group of about 80 people including Rudetzki on the investigation's progress, she said.
The Armed Islamic Group (GIA) has claimed responsibility for the 1995 bomb attacks, accusing France of siding with Algeria's military government in a civil war against Moslem rebels.

The GIA said its attacks were also intended to avenge the deaths of four of its members in the December 1994 hijacking of an Air France airliner. French commandos killed the hijackers as they stormed the plane to free their 169 hostages.
No one has claimed responsibility for the single 1996 attack, on an underground train at Paris' Port Royal station.

Bensaid was arrested in the northern city of Lille in November 1995 along with nine other suspects. He has been kept in custody under French laws permitting suspects in terrorism-related crimes to be held for long, regularly renewable periods while an investigation is continuing.

Investigators have said they believe he worked on the Saint Michel attack with Ali Touchent, an Algerian architecture student also known as "Tarek" whose whereabouts are unknown, and Khaled Kelkal, a young Frenchman of Algerian origin who was shot dead by police near Lyon, central France, in September 1995.

He was also in telephone contact with Algerian Rachid Ramda, suspected by French investigators of having helped plan the 1995 bombing wave from his residence in London, according to Roland Jacquard, president of the Paris-based International Observatory on Terrorism. France is currently seeking to extradite Ramda.

Jacquard further told Reuters that a GIA activist, arrested on French soil in November 1995, has told investigators that Bensaid boasted to him of his involvement in preparing for the Saint Michel attack.
Bensaid's fingerprints have been found on two bombs linked to Algerian rebel groups operating in France, investigators say.

One, which failed to go off, was found next to a high-speed TGV passenger train line linking Paris and Lyon in August 1995. The second blew up near an entrance to the Maison Blanche Metro underground station in Paris in October 1995, injuring 13.
Several Algerian rebel groups including the GIA have vowed to topple the Algerian government and transform the north African state into an Islamic republic.
An estimated 60,000 people have died in civil strife in Algeria since authorities there cancelled a general election in 1992 that the fundamentalists were poised to win.
